title: 4 Best AI Prompts for Writing Unit Tests (2026)
description: Generate tests that actually catch bugs — behavior mapping, edge-case tables, implementation, and a mutation check — not just coverage padding.

steps.title: Map the behaviors, not the functions
steps.promptText:
Here is the code to test:
[PASTE CODE]

Before writing any tests, list every observable behavior a caller relies on: inputs → outputs, side effects, thrown errors, and ordering guarantees. Format: behavior | trigger | expected result | how likely a refactor breaks it (high/med/low). Include behaviors that are implied but not obvious from signatures.
steps.whyThisTool: Testing behaviors instead of functions is the difference between a safety net and coverage theater.
steps.outputExpected: A behavior inventory — usually 2-3 behaviors you hadn't consciously registered.

steps.title: Build the edge-case table
steps.promptText: For each high-risk behavior above, enumerate edge cases: empty/null/undefined, boundaries (0, 1, max, max+1), unicode and whitespace strings, concurrent calls, and invalid types. Output a table: case | input | expected. Mark which cases the current code probably FAILS — be honest.
steps.whyThisTool: The 'probably fails' column turns test writing into bug hunting.
steps.outputExpected: An edge-case table with predicted failures worth checking first.

steps.title: Write the tests
steps.promptText: Write the tests in [FRAMEWORK] covering every behavior and edge case above. Rules: one behavior per test, names that describe the scenario ("rejects_expired_token_with_401" not "test_auth_2"), arrange-act-assert structure, no mocking anything you don't own, and no testing private internals.
steps.whyThisTool: Explicit test-quality rules stop AI from generating the brittle mock-everything suites it defaults to.
steps.outputExpected: A test file you'd approve in review — readable names, real assertions, minimal mocks.

steps.title: Mutation-check your suite
steps.promptText: Now act as a mutation tester: list 5 specific small bugs you could introduce into the original code (flip a comparison, off-by-one a boundary, swallow an error) and for EACH one say which test would catch it — or admit none would. Write the missing tests for any survivors.
steps.whyThisTool: Mutation thinking is the cheapest way to measure whether tests actually protect anything.
steps.outputExpected: Either 'all mutants caught' or the exact tests you were missing.

faq.a: The main flakiness sources are over-mocking and timing assumptions — step 3's rules ban the first and surface the second. Still review anything involving time, network, or randomness.

faq.q: What frameworks does this work with?
faq.a: Any — Jest, Vitest, pytest, JUnit, go test. Name yours in step 3 and the conventions adapt.
No. The goal is that the mutation check in step 4 comes back 'caught'. Coverage is a side effect, not the target.

benefit: Catch the edge-case bugs your current tests silently miss.
